units.spoken: Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG): Actor and Critic
One network sets a robot arm's turning forces; a second scores them and shows which way to change them.

sections.section: 1 Many robot arms reaching for a moving goal

units.spoken: Section one, Many robot arms reaching for a moving goal
A robot arm needs four real-numbered turning forces at its joints every step, and the Deep Q-Network (DQN) can only pick from a list.
A short list of levels makes the arm jerky, and a fine list with many levels grows huge.
Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) trains one network to output the forces and a second to score them.

One step shows all five words at once: the agent is the learner that picks the moves, a state is the agent's situation right now, a move, or action, is one choice the agent can make in a state, a reward is the number the world hands back after each move, good or bad, and an episode is one run from the start until it ends.
1.1 The Reacher arm

The running example is the Reacher task: a robot arm with two joints whose actions are four torques. A torque is a turning force a motor applies at a joint. On the Reacher each torque is a number from -1 to 1. Each joint can turn about two axes, so each joint gets two torques. Every step the arm senses its state: 33 numbers covering where its parts sit, how they are turned, and how fast they move and spin. The arm earns a small reward whenever its hand is inside a moving goal. The code comes from RF-DDPG, a public repo on GitHub, which trains 20 such arms side by side.

Take a look at this figure. The arm has two joints, a shoulder and an elbow, each turning about two axes. Four torques, one per axis, turn the joints. The hand hangs just short of the goal ball. The lesson is the task: turn the joints so the hand lands on the moving goal.

The Reacher arm the whole page returns to has two joints, four torques, and a goal that moves. With the hand hanging just short of the goal, a small turn at the shoulder and the elbow together brings it onto the goal.
1.2 One loop around the arm

Take a look at this figure. The loop runs in a circle: the arm's state goes to a network that writes the torques, the torques move the arm, and a second network scores the state and torques and says which way the score rises. A dashed arrow carries that uphill direction back to the actor. The lesson is the loop: the score alone tells the actor which torques to keep.

The loop runs from state to torques to arm to score: the state goes to a network that writes the torques, the torques move the arm, and the critic says which way the score rises. The dashed arrow carries the critic's uphill direction back to the actor. The loop matters because the score alone tells the actor which torques to keep. With the hand short of the goal, one pass writes new torques and raises the score.
1.3 What counts as solved

A step with the hand on the goal earns a small reward, any other step earns nothing. The total reward is averaged over all 20 arms and over a long run of episodes, so one lucky arm or one lucky episode cannot pass the bar.
The return is all the reward still to come, with later rewards counted a little less.
The task counts as solved once the average return passes 30, the solve bar. Early on the hand circles and earns almost no reward; late in training it stays on the goal.

Take a look at this figure. The simulation and the agent pass numbers back and forth: the simulation sends the arm's 33 numbers and a reward down, and the agent sends four torques back up. The agent reads numbers, not pixels. The lesson is the step: the agent learns only from what the simulation sends back.

One step runs both ways between the simulation and the agent: the simulation sends the arm's state and a reward down, and the agent sends four torques back up. The step matters because the agent learns only from what the simulation sends back. With the hand on the goal, the step returns a small reward, and the agent sends torques that hold the hand there.

This code steps the arms with random torques. It resets all 20 arms, reads each arm's state, and draws random torques from minus one to one until any episode ends, adding up the rewards. The lesson is the starting point: with random torques, the arms earn almost no reward.

1. The listings use the Unity ML-Agents Reacher environment. Unity is the game engine the simulation runs in, and ML-Agents is the toolkit that trains agents inside it. A brain is the decision maker ML-Agents attaches to the arms: brain_name is the first brain's name, the handle the snippet uses to read the arms. env is the simulation itself. The snippet resets all 20 arms, reads each arm's state from vector_observations, the 33 numbers per arm, and checks local_done, the flag that says whether an arm's episode has ended.
2. Steps the arms with random torques in minus one to one until any episode ends, adding up rewards.

sections.section: 2 Why DQN cannot drive the arm

units.spoken: Section two, Why DQN cannot drive the arm
The deterministic actor
What. Picture the arm's state going into one network and four torques coming straight out, no list, no search.
How. The network reads the 33 state numbers and writes one torque per joint axis.
Why. The same state always gives the same four torques, and the hand lands closer to the goal each time.
A list of torque levels makes the arm jerky, and the list soon grows too long to search.

Each move the arm can make has a value: Q of s and a, also called its score, is the return the agent expects if it makes move a in state s and plays on from there. A Q-table keeps one score for every state and move.
The arm's joint angles and speeds can take endless values, so such a table could never list them all.
DQN swaps the table for a network that takes the state and outputs one score per move.
DDPG replaces that search with a network.

Each state needs a rule for choosing a move, and that rule is the policy: it may always pick the same move or pick by chance. The deterministic actor mu sub thay-ta is a network with weights thay-ta that outputs one action every time, with no random draw.

Equation 1. DQN picks from a list, and the arm needs four real-numbered torques at every step, so no list can hold them all. A robot arm reaching for a goal must set each joint torque by an exact amount, not pick a level off a list.
Take a look at this equation. DQN picks the best move off a list, and the actor writes the torques straight from the state, with no list at all.

The first line. A star is the best move, the star on top marking the winner. Argmax sub a searches the list of allowed moves and returns the one with the biggest score, not the score itself. Q of s and a is the move's value, the score of move a in state s, the return the agent expects if it makes that move there and plays on. A star equals argmax sub a of Q of s and a. Intuitively, a list can only hold moves somebody wrote down, and a fine list grows too long to search.
Intuition. A list can only hold moves somebody wrote down, and a fine list grows too long to search.
Example. With a short list of torque levels on one joint, the best level on the list still leaves the hand short of the goal, because no level lands exactly on it.

The second line. A is the action, the four torques, each from minus one to one. Mu sub thay-ta is the actor, a network with weights thay-ta. S is the state, the arm's 33 numbers. A equals mu sub thay-ta of s. Intuitively, the actor writes the torques straight out, with no search and no list.
Intuition. The actor skips the search entirely and writes the torques straight from the state.
Example. For one state where the elbow torque needs a nudge, the actor writes the four torques at once, with no search over levels.
So DQN picks the best move off a list, and the actor writes the torques straight from the state, with no list to search.

Take a look at this figure. On the left, DQN picks from a list of buttons, one per torque level, and argmax takes the best one. On the right, the actor outputs a torque directly, any value from minus one to one, with no list and no search. The lesson is the gap: one torque the arm needs sits between two buttons, so no button lands on it.
One torque the arm needs sits between two buttons, so no button lands on it, while the actor writes it exactly.

sections.section: 3 An actor network and a critic network

units.spoken: Section three, An actor network and a critic network
The critic scores the torques
What. Picture a second network beside the actor, reading the state and the torques together and answering with one score.
How. It scores each state and action pair by the return it expects from there.
Why. Better torques score higher, so the score tells the actor which way to move its torques.
The actor needs a second network to tell it which torques are good.
The critic Q sub fee is a network with weights fee that scores a state and an action together; its score stands for the return the agent expects.

For the Reacher the action is the arm's four torques. The state goes through a first hidden layer, a row of units that turns the state numbers into a shorter summary, then the critic joins the four torques to it, and the last layer turns them into one score.

Take a look at this figure. Two networks with opposite jobs. The actor reads the state only and writes the torques, squashed into the torque range, the same torques every time for the same state. The critic reads the state first, then joins the torques to it, and answers with one score. The lesson is the split: the actor proposes, the critic judges, and the critic never picks actions.
For one state, the actor writes its torques, and the critic scores that state with those torques.

This code builds the actor as a stack of layers: the state goes in, hidden layers turn it into a shorter summary, and a tanh at the end squashes the four torques into minus one to one. The lesson is the shape: 33 numbers in, four torques out.
1. The sizes are the Reacher's: 33 state numbers in, 4 torques out, hidden layers 256, 128, 64. The tanh function squashes any number into minus one to one, the torque range.

This code builds the critic. The state goes through a first layer on its own, then the four torques join it, and the last layer turns them into one score. The lesson is the order: the state goes first, and the torques join after the first layer.
1. Builds the layers with the sizes the actor snippet sets; the action joins after the first layer.
2. Encodes the state, appends the four torques, and outputs one score.
The DDPG paper by Lillicrap and coauthors, from 2016, is the source for the two networks this page teaches.
Exploration noise is a small random nudge added to the actor's actions while it learns, so the agent tries moves it is not sure about.

sections.section: 4 Training the critic from stored steps

units.spoken: Section four, Training the critic from stored steps
The critic learns from stored steps
What. Picture the critic pulled toward a target that barely moves, the reward plus the discounted slow score of what comes next.
How. The loss is the mean squared error: each stored step contributes its squared gap between score and target, averaged over the batch.
Why. The scores move toward their targets a little at a time, and the critic judges new torques against targets that barely move.

Replay keeps a memory of past steps, and training draws random batches from it. The critic learns from random batches of these steps, so it does not learn only from the arm's last few moves. That makes DDPG off-policy: it learns from steps an exploring actor took, the same actor with exploration noise added, not only from steps its current actor would take. It is also model-free: it learns from the arm's steps alone, with no model of what the arm will do next.
The critic learns by being pulled toward a target, the step's reward plus its own score for what comes next, counted a little less. That target moves whenever the critic moves.
The discount gamma sets how much a reward one step later still counts. A discount close to 1 keeps far rewards almost fully; a small one counts mostly the reward just earned.

The target network is a slow copy of the Q-network, with weights fee prime, that computes the targets. DQN introduced the target network, but DQN refreshes its copy in one jump every so often, while DDPG blends its copy a little at a time, a step called a soft update. In DDPG's actor-critic family the critic plays the Q-network's part.

In DDPG both the actor and the critic have a slow copy, marked by a prime on the weights, and the targets are built from those copies. DQN's target takes a max, the highest of the scores its Q-network gives the next moves.

Batch normalization steadies training alongside replay and the slow copies: it rescales each layer's inputs across the batch to a steady mean and spread. The listings on this page leave it out: neither network uses a normalization layer.
Equation 2. The critic learns by aiming its scores at a target built from slow copies, so the target barely moves while the critic learns.
Take a look at this equation. The critic's target is the reward plus the discounted slow score of what comes next, built from slow copies so it barely moves.

The target line. Why is the target the critic's scores are pulled toward. Ar is the reward; the plus adds what comes next. Gamma is the discount, so a later reward counts less. Q sub fee prime is the slow critic, the prime marking the slow copy. Inside it sit s prime, the next state, and mu sub thay-ta prime of s prime, the slow actor's next torques, the prime marking the slow actor. Why equals ar plus gamma times Q sub fee prime of s prime and mu sub thay-ta prime of s prime. Intuitively, the slow copies barely move, so the target barely moves.
Intuition. A target built from the critic's own moving scores shifts with every update, so the critic needs one that barely moves.
Example. For a stored step where the hand just missed the goal, the reward is zero, so the target is the discount times the slow score of the next torques, with no reward added.
So the target is the reward plus the discounted slow score of the slow actor's next torques, and the slow copies barely move, so the target barely moves.

For a stored step where the hand sits on the goal, the reward is plus 0.1, and the next state puts the hand just off it, so the target is that reward plus the discounted slow score of the slow actor's next torques. Because the slow copies barely move, the same stored step keeps nearly the same target while the critic learns.

Equation 3 pulls the critic's score for each stored step toward its target. The gap between a target and a guess is the TD error: TD stands for temporal difference, the difference between two guesses a step apart.

A batch is a handful of remembered steps trained on together; the loss averages how far their scores are from their targets, an average of squared gaps called the mean squared error. A minibatch is the same thing: one batch drawn from the memory.

Equation 3. The critic's scores are only useful if training can measure how far they sit from their targets. The hand short of the goal scores less than the hand on it, and the loss measures how far each score sits from its target.
Take a look at this equation. The critic's loss is the average squared gap between its scores and their targets, so training pulls every score toward its target.

The loss line. L of fee is the loss for the critic's weights fee. Changing fee changes the scores, so it changes the loss. E, the expectation, averages the batch: add the squared gaps over the steps, then divide by their number. Inside it sits why minus Q sub fee of s and a, the whole bracket squared. Why is the target, the reward plus the discounted slow score of what comes next. Q sub fee of s and a is the critic's score for the stored torques in state s. The minus takes the score away from the target, so the gap is the TD error. The square makes the gap always positive, so a miss counts either way and big misses count more. Intuitively, the critic improves only by seeing the gap between its score and its target.
termList: Q sub fee of s and a

units.spoken: Intuition. The critic improves only by seeing the gap between its score and its target.
Example. For a stored step whose score sits above its target, the squared gap still counts, so the next update pulls that score down toward its target.
So the loss is the batch average of the squared gaps, and training pulls every score toward its target.

This code builds the target and moves the critic. The target function asks the slow actor for the next torques and the slow critic for their score, then returns the reward plus the discounted slow score, with nothing added where an episode ended. The update function pulls the critic's scores toward those targets by mean squared error, caps the step, and steps the optimizer. The lesson is the loop: build the target from slow copies, then pull the scores toward it.
1. The flag keep is zero where an arm's episode ended, so no future value is added there.

2. Moves the critic toward why, the target, by mean squared error, and the clip call caps its step at a gradient norm of 1. learn() in DDPG's full loop in PyTorch calls it, and the setup block there creates the critic, its optimizer, the discount, and the two target copies.
The slow copies move by one rule: each slow weight takes a small share of its live weight after every update.
Equation 5. The slow copies blend toward the networks a little at a time, so the targets built from them barely move.
Take a look at this equation. Each slow copy blends a small share of its live network after every update, so the targets barely move.

The first line, the slow critic. Fee prime is the slow critic's weights, the copy that builds the critic's targets. The arrow replaces the left side with the right side. Tau times fee is a small share of the live critic's weights: tau is the share blended per update, 0.001 in the repo. The plus adds one minus tau times fee prime, the rest of the slow copy's own. Fee prime gets replaced by tau times fee plus one minus tau times fee prime. One minus tau is what stays, so the two shares add to one, a weighted average. With tau small, each slow weight moves only a hair per update, while DQN's hard copy blends in all of the live weights at once. Intuitively, the slow copy creeps toward the live network instead of jumping to it.
Intuition. The target the critic learns from must barely move while the critic learns, so the slow copy creeps toward the live network instead of jumping to it.

Example. For one slow critic weight after an update on a Reacher batch, the live critic's matching weight has shifted a little while learning, and the slow copy takes only a small share of that shift, so the target the critic learns from next barely moves.

The second line, the slow actor. Thay-ta prime is the slow actor's weights, the copy whose next torques the slow critic scores. The blend takes tau times thay-ta, a small share of the live actor's weights, plus one minus tau times thay-ta prime, the rest of its own. Tau is the same share, so the actor's copy trails at the same slow pace. Intuitively, both slow copies sit inside the critic's target, so after each update the targets move slowly instead of chasing the live networks.
Intuition. The slow actor trails the same way as the slow critic, so the torques the target scores stay close to the ones it scored before.

Example. For one slow actor weight after an update, the live actor's matching weight has shifted a little, and the slow copy takes only a small share of that shift, so the slow actor's next torques barely change.
So both slow copies blend a small share of their live networks after each update, and the targets move slowly instead of chasing the live networks.

sections.section: 5 Moving the actor uphill on the critic

units.spoken: Section five, Moving the actor uphill on the critic
The actor climbs the critic's slope
What. Picture the critic's slope under the actor's torques, pointing uphill toward the peak.
How. The slope is turned into a change in the actor's weights, so the next torques shift toward higher scores.
Why. Each update writes torques a little closer to the peak, and the hand spends more time on the goal.

Take a look at this figure. The critic's score draws a curve over one torque, for one fixed state. A dot marks the actor's output now, and an arrow points uphill along the slope toward the peak. The lesson is the direction: the slope is the only direction the actor has, and each update steps the dot uphill.

The critic's score draws a curve over one torque, for one fixed state. The dot is the actor's output now, and the arrow points uphill along the slope toward the peak. The curve matters because its slope is the only direction the actor has. With one torque low on the curve, the slope points up toward the peak.
A policy gradient is any rule that moves the actor's weights to raise the return; this one is deterministic because the actor has no random draw.

Equation 4. The critic can score torques but cannot pick them, so the actor needs a way to turn the critic's slope into a change in its own weights. The actor reads the slope at the torques it just wrote, and needs that slope as a change in its weights.
Take a look at this equation. The critic's slope at the actor's torques becomes a change in the actor's weights, so the next torques shift uphill.

The first line, the slope. Gee is the uphill direction, the critic's slope. Nabla sub a is the gradient with respect to the action: it asks how the score changes when the torques change, not when the weights change. Q sub fee of s and a is the critic's score of the torques a in state s, taken at the actor's pick: the bar fixes the torques at mu sub thay-ta of s, the actor's torques from the state. Gee equals Nabla sub a of Q sub fee of s and a. Intuitively, the critic knows which way is uphill, but only the actor can move.
termList: Q sub fee of s and a

units.spoken: Intuition. The critic knows which way is uphill, but only the actor can move.
Example. For one torque on the low side of the curve, the slope points up the curve, toward the peak.

The second line, the weight change. Nabla sub thay-ta Jay is the uphill direction in the actor's weights, raising its expected return Jay. Jay is the expected return, the average return over the many runs the actor could have from here, not the reward of one run. Approximately says the exact version would average over states the current actor itself would visit, while this version averages over stored states from the exploring actor. This rule is Silver and coauthors' deterministic policy gradient theorem: the average runs over states only, because the actor writes one set of torques per state instead of picking by chance. E, the expectation, is the batch average: add each step's product, then divide by their number. Rho super beta is the spread of states the exploring actor visits, and beta is the exploring policy, the actor plus its exploration noise. In the paper the average runs over states from rho super beta, the states the exploring actor visits, and the batch of stored steps stands in for them. Gee is the critic's slope, and Nabla sub thay-ta mu sub thay-ta of s is how the torques move with the weights. The product is the chain rule, the rule that chains two slopes together: torque slope times how the torques move with the weights is the weight slope. Nabla sub thay-ta Jay is approximately the expected value of gee times Nabla sub thay-ta mu sub thay-ta of s. Intuitively, the slope at the actor's torques becomes a change in the weights that write them.
termList: Nabla sub thay-ta mu sub thay-ta of s

units.spoken: Intuition. The slope at the actor's torques becomes a change in the weights that write them.
Example. For one batch of stored steps, each step contributes its own slope product, and the average points the weights uphill.
So the critic's slope becomes a change in the actor's weights, and each update writes torques a little closer to the peak.

This code moves the actor. It takes the states of one batch, scores the actor's torques with the critic, and sets the actor's loss to minus that score, so raising the score lowers the loss. The lesson is the trick: the actor climbs by making the critic's score bigger.
1. Takes the states of the same batch; the actor's loss is minus the critic's score of its action, and the mean is the average over the batch.

2. Updates only the actor. The actor's loss is minus the critic's score of the actor's action, so the backward pass runs through the critic too and leaves gradients on the critic's weights; critic_update zeroes them before the critic's next step. learn() in DDPG's full loop in PyTorch calls it, and actor_opt is created there.

sections.section: 6 One DDPG step on the arm

units.spoken: Section six, One DDPG step on the arm
One DDPG step
What. Picture one loop around the arm: act, store, draw a batch, build targets, move the critic, then move the actor.
How. The critic learns from the batch first, then its slope moves the actor.
Why. One step leaves both networks a little better, and the next step starts from a better arm.

Take a look at this figure. One DDPG step runs as a loop around the arm: the actor writes the torques, the arm stores the step, and the critic teaches the actor. The actor acts, the step is stored, a batch is drawn, targets are built, the critic moves, then the actor moves. The lesson is the order: the critic learns from the batch first, then its slope moves the actor.

One DDPG update runs as a loop around the arm: the actor acts, the arm stores the step, and the critic teaches the actor. For a stored step whose hand reached the goal, its target carries the reward, the critic moves toward it, and the next torques shift toward higher scores.

Try the walkthrough. Press Play to run one DDPG step through the walk, or step through it with Next. Watch the actor write the torques, the target build from the slow copies, the critic loss pull the scores toward the targets, and the actor update move the weights uphill. Each stage lights the matching part of the equation card. Press Reset to start the walk again.
Tool 1: One DDPG step

One DDPG step runs the whole update on one batch: the actor writes the torques, the target is built from the slow copies, the critic loss pulls the scores toward the targets, and the actor update moves the weights uphill. The slow copies blend toward the networks after each update in the full loop.
Take a look at this walkthrough. It follows one DDPG step through the whole update, from the actor writing the torques to the actor's weights moving uphill.
The first line. A is the actor's torques, mu sub thay-ta is the actor, and s is the state. A equals mu sub thay-ta of s.
The actor writes the torques.

The second line. Why is the target, ar is the reward, gamma is the discount, and Q sub fee prime of s prime and mu sub thay-ta prime of s prime is the slow score of what comes next. Why equals ar plus gamma times that slow score.
The reward starts the target.
The slow copies add what comes next.
The third line. L of fee is the critic's loss, E averages the batch, and why minus Q sub fee of s and a, squared, is each step's gap. L of fee equals E of the squared gaps.

units.spoken: The loss measures how far each score sits from its target.
The gaps are squared and averaged over the batch.
The fourth line. Gee is the critic's slope, Nabla sub a asks how the score changes when the torques change, and Q sub fee of s and a is the critic's score at the actor's pick.

units.spoken: The critic reports which way each torque should change.
The fifth line. Nabla sub thay-ta Jay is the uphill direction in the actor's weights, gee is the critic's slope, and Nabla sub thay-ta mu sub thay-ta of s is how the torques move with the weights.

sections.section: 7 The step size and the false peak

units.spoken: Section seven, The step size and the false peak
Climbing and the false peak
What. Picture a dot climbing the critic's curve, stopping where the slope flattens, even on a small false peak short of the true one.
How. Each update steps the dot uphill by the step size, and it stops where the slope is flat.
Why. The dot reaches the true peak; when the critic draws a false bump, it stops short, and that is the failure to watch.

Take a look at this figure. The critic's curve carries a false bump partway up: it rises to a small hump, dips, then rises to the true peak. The dot climbs the hump and stops there because the slope flattens. The lesson is the failure: with a false bump, the torque stops on the false peak, short of the true peak.

When the critic's curve carries a false bump partway up, the curve rises to a small hump, dips, then rises to the true peak, and the dot climbs the hump and stops there because the slope flattens. Tool 2 adds the bump with its 'accurate critic' button. With the smallest step and the bump on, the dot stops on the false peak, short of the true peak.

Try the tool. Move the step size slider and watch the dot climb the critic's curve. Turn on the accurate critic button to add the false bump, and watch the dot stop on the false peak with the smallest step. The learning rate eta sets how big a step each update takes: here eta is the dot's step size on the slider, not the optimizer rate of 0.001 in DDPG's full loop in PyTorch. The lesson is the trap: a false bump stops the climb short of the true peak.
Tool 2: Climbing the critic's curve
Section eight, DDPG's full loop in PyTorch

Take a look at this figure. The training cadence runs in three numbered rows: acting never stops, updates run in bursts, and the slow copies catch up a little. The long bar is acting and storing every step, the orange ticks are bursts of updates, and the green ticks are the slow copies blending. The lesson is the rhythm: act and store for a while, then run a burst of updates.

The training cadence runs in three numbered rows: acting never stops, updates run in bursts, and the slow copies catch up a little. The long blue bar is acting and storing every step, the orange ticks are bursts of updates, and the green ticks are the slow copies blending after each update. For one cycle, the arms act and store for a while, then a burst of updates runs, and the slow copies move a little toward the networks being trained.
An update is one gradient step on one sampled batch.

Learning runs in bursts so each stored step gets reused many times: the arms act and store for a while, then a burst of updates trains on old steps. Overfit means the critic fits the sampled steps too closely and stops judging new torques well. This burst cadence is the repo's: the paper's Algorithm 1 updates the networks at every step instead.

The code in this section runs the schedule of Figure 9: act and store every step 1, and every so often learn in a burst of updates on random batches 2, each followed by the slow copies moving a little toward the networks being trained 3.
8.1 Networks, settings and slow copies

This code sets up the training run. It imports the pieces, reads the first brain of the Reacher, builds the critic and a slow target copy of each network, pairs each target with its live network, and creates an Adam optimizer for each network. It sets the discount and the slow-copy share, and opens the memory for stored steps and a record of recent returns.
1. Imports for the buffer, the target copies and the optimizers.
2. The settings, from the repo: the slow-copy share tau is 0.001, the share of the live weights each slow copy takes in per update.
3. The setup block reads the first brain of the Unity ML-Agents Reacher environment.
4. Makes the critic from the Critic class, a slow target copy of each network, and pairs to match each target copy with its live network.
5. An Adam optimizer (a gradient step that adapts its size per weight) for each network, plus the discount and the share of the live weights each slow copy takes in per update.
6. The memory holds the stored steps, and a record of the recent episode returns.
8.2 Storing steps and blending slow copies

This code turns rows into tensors, stores steps, and blends the slow copies. One function turns a list of rows into a tensor of decimal numbers. Another stores one transition per arm: state, torques, reward, next state, and the episode-end flag. The third moves every target weight a share of the way toward its live weight. The lesson is the plumbing: store every step, and nudge the slow copies after each update.
1. Turns a list of rows into one tensor of decimal numbers, for the actor and for sampled batches.

2. Stores one transition per arm: a transition is one stored step holding state, torques, reward, next state, and episode-end flag. The code calls the next state obs, short for observation, and returns the next states.
3. Moves every target weight a share of the way toward its live weight.
8.3 One learning burst

This code runs one learning burst. It waits until the memory holds more than one batch, draws a random batch, and makes the five tensors. Then it runs the critic update and the actor update on that batch, and nudges both target copies a little toward their live networks. The lesson is the burst: one batch, two updates, then the slow copies catch up.
1. Waits until the memory holds more than one batch.
2. Draws a random batch and makes the five tensors, one row per sampled step; r and done become one column so they match the critic's one-score output.
3. Runs critic_update, then actor_update, on this batch. The gradient norm is the size of the step the gradient asks for, so the repo caps each critic step at a gradient norm of 1.
4. Nudges both target copies a little toward their live networks.
8.4 The loop that acts, stores and learns

This code runs the loop that acts, stores, and learns. It runs until the average return passes the solve bar. Each episode resets the arms, and every step all 20 arms act and store one transition each. Every so often a burst of updates runs. The lesson is the whole run: act and store, learn in bursts, until the hand stays on the goal.
1. The loop runs until the average return passes the solve bar.
2. Each episode resets all the arms and zeroes their total rewards; step counts steps across episodes.
3. Every step all 20 arms act and store one transition each. The repo adds exploration noise, a small random nudge so the arm tries new moves, inside its act step, which this listing leaves out.
4. Every so often, a burst of updates runs.

The repo's run on the 20-arm Reacher passed the bar: the average return over the last 100 episodes passed 30, so late in training the hand stayed on the goal. The training curve climbs from near zero, crosses the solve bar, dips back once, and then holds above it. The paper solved more than 20 simulated physics tasks with one algorithm, one architecture and one set of settings.

sections.section: 9 When DDPG fits and how it fails

units.spoken: Section nine, When DDPG fits and how it fails
DDPG fits when actions are continuous, old steps must be reused, and the task needs only a simple actor-critic.

DDPG explores only through noise, of a kind chosen by hand, added to the actor's chosen torques, and without that noise the arm may never find the goal. The paper says the noise can be chosen to suit the environment.
Twin Delayed DDPG (TD3), a later method, keeps two critics and takes the lower score, so the actor stops chasing scores that are too high.
Soft Actor-Critic (SAC), another later method, rewards the actor for staying unpredictable as well as for scoring high, so it learns how much to explore instead of relying on hand-tuned noise.
The first failure is the critic scoring too high, and the actor chases those scores.

Why does the paper's version of DDPG pair slow copies, a replay memory and batch normalization? Slow copies steady the targets, replay draws old steps into each batch, and batch normalization steadies each layer's inputs. Together they make the paper's training reliable. Even with all three, training may never settle.
